Right, I am writing down the brisket properly this time because every cook does it differently and last week it came out grey. This is the one we put on when the market has the cheap end cuts, not the braise on the menu, and the difference is that this one gets a dry rub the night before and the menu one does not. Buy the whole piece with the fat cap on, and do not let them trim it for you, because they always take too much and then it dries out in the second hour. What goes in the rub. Coarse salt. Black pepper, cracked, not ground. Brown sugar. Smoked paprika. Ground fennel. The proportions are not fussy but the salt has to be more than you think, roughly a heaped tablespoon for a piece that size, and the sugar is there for colour more than sweetness so if it looks like a lot it probably is not. You rub it the night before and you leave it uncovered on a tray in the cold room, because the surface needs to dry out, and if you cover it you get a wet skin and no crust. Then in the morning you take it out an hour before it goes in the oven, and you do not rinse it, people always want to rinse it and it undoes the whole point. The oven goes low, and I mean genuinely low, and then you leave it alone for the first three hours, and after that you start looking at it every forty minutes or so, and when the fat has gone soft and the thin end feels loose you put the foil on and you keep going until the middle gives way when you push a spoon into it. If it stalls, and it will stall, that is normal and it is not the oven, so do not turn the heat up because you will tighten the meat and you will not get it back. The resting is the part everybody rushes. It needs a full hour out of the oven, loosely covered, somewhere out of a draught, and it will not go cold in that time, and if you slice it early all the liquid runs out onto the board and the pieces fall apart in the pass. Slice it against the grain and slice it thicker than you would for the menu one, because the fibres are shorter after this long a cook and thin slices just collapse. The sauce is whatever is in the tray, poured off, left to settle for ten minutes, and then the fat lifted off the top, and it needs nothing else in it. If the tray has caught, and only if it has caught, put a little of the stock in and scrape it while it is still hot, but taste it first because caught sugar turns bitter quickly and you cannot take that back out. And write on the card that this one needs starting two days before service, not one, because the rub night is not optional and every time somebody has tried to shortcut it we have ended up serving something that tastes fine and looks wrong, and then I get asked why it is not the same as last month.

Okay, this is the write up for the collector change and it is going to be longer than usual because the reviewer is probably going to be somebody who has never touched this service. The symptom is that the dashboard shows gaps of between forty seconds and two minutes, always on the hour, and always on the hosts that carry the most traffic. Support has three tickets about it and two of them are from the same customer, who noticed that their alert did not fire during a real outage, which is why I am not treating this as cosmetic. What is actually happening is that the collector rotates its output file on the hour and it does the rotation on the same thread that accepts writes, so while the rotation is in progress the accept path blocks, and on a busy host the rotation takes long enough that the upstream buffer fills and starts dropping. On a quiet host it finishes in under a second and nobody sees anything, which is why this never reproduced in staging and why we spent two weeks blaming the network. The change does three things and I want them read in this order. First it moves the rotation onto its own thread so the accept path never waits on file system work. Second it makes the buffer drop policy explicit and counted so that a drop is visible instead of being inferred from a hole in a graph. Third it adds a metric for rotation duration, because I do not want the next person to have to reconstruct this from timestamps the way I did. Testing was mostly load based rather than unit based and I would rather say that plainly than dress it up. I ran the collector under synthetic load at roughly three times the peak rate we see on the busiest host, for six hours, with rotation forced every five minutes instead of hourly, and there were no gaps and no drops at all. I also ran the same shape of test against the old build to confirm that it fails the way I claim it fails, and it does, reliably, inside the first two rotations. There are unit tests for the drop counter and for the rotation duration metric, but there is no unit test for the threading change itself, because I could not write one that would fail for the right reason rather than by luck. What I have not done is test any of this on the ARM hosts, because I do not have access to them, and somebody who does should run it there before this goes past canary. I also have not touched the reader side at all, so if there are historical gaps already written into old files then this does nothing about those, and the support tickets will need a separate answer about the data we have already lost. I want to get this out of my head before the review, because I am going to be the person arguing against the change and I would rather have thought about it properly than just react in the meeting. The proposal is to rename everything in the storage layer so that the field names match the API, which in practice means the database goes from snake case to camel case across about forty tables. I understand why it is being proposed. Every new person who joins spends their first fortnight writing a mapping in their head, and there are three places in the codebase where somebody got it wrong and the bug was invisible until a customer noticed, so the cost is real and it is not only aesthetics. My problem is the size of the blast radius against the size of the benefit. The database is not the only consumer. There are two reporting jobs that were written before I joined and neither of them goes through the ORM, they read the tables directly with hand written SQL, and the person who wrote them left in twenty twenty three. There is also the export that the finance team runs at month end, which produces a file whose headers are the raw column names, and somebody downstream of us has a spreadsheet with formulas that reference those headers both by position and by name. I know that is fragile and I know it is not our problem in theory, but the last time we changed a header we found out about it eleven days later from a very unhappy email. If we are going to do this then I think it has to be done as a view layer first, so the old names keep working while the new ones exist, and then we remove the old names in a separate change once we can prove nobody is reading them. That is more work and it is less satisfying, but it is the only version of this that I would sign off on. What I do not want is the version where we rename the columns, fix everything that breaks in the test suite, ship it, and then spend a month finding the things the test suite cannot see. The other thing I keep coming back to is that camel case in the database does not actually solve the mapping problem, it moves it, because the API is not the only interface we have. The event stream uses kebab case for topic names and screaming snake case for the header keys, and nobody is proposing to change those, so a new person still has three conventions to hold in their head instead of two. If the goal is to reduce the number of conventions then the honest version of this proposal is much bigger than the storage layer, and if the goal is only to make the ORM mapping file shorter then we should say that out loud and weigh it against a month of migration risk. Either way I am not against it in principle, I am against doing it in one step.

Long note on the stock reconciliation, because I have been asked for it twice and I want one version of it that I can point at. The headline is that the system count and the physical count disagree by about four per cent by value, and almost none of that four per cent is theft, which is what everybody assumes when they hear a variance number. Start with what the four per cent is made of. Just over half of it is the returns process. A return is booked back into stock at the moment the label is scanned at the depot, but the item does not become sellable until somebody inspects it, and the gap between those two events averages nine days. So for nine days the system believes we have an item that we cannot sell, and if the count happens in those nine days the item is present, sellable in the system, and physically sitting in a cage waiting for a decision. Second piece is the multipack problem. Some products are sold both singly and in packs of six, and the pack is a separate code that decrements six of the single code when it ships. If somebody breaks a pack on the shop floor and sells the units individually, which happens because customers ask, then the single code goes negative and the pack code stays high, and the two errors are the same size and opposite sign so they cancel in the total and both show up in the by line detail. That is why the summary looks better than the detail, and anybody who has only ever seen the summary thinks the detail is broken. Third piece, and this is the smallest but the one that generates the most email, is the transfers. A transfer between the two sites is a single transaction in the system and two events in reality, and if the receiving site does not confirm on the same day then for a period the stock exists in neither place. Over a month there are maybe forty of those and each one is small. What I want to change. The returns booking should happen at inspection and not at scan, which is a configuration change rather than a project, and on its own it takes the variance from four per cent to under two. The multipack thing needs a rule that a pack cannot be broken without a transaction, and that is a training problem more than a systems one. The transfers I would leave alone for now because the effort is high and the amount is trivial. One thing I want to be careful about in how this gets presented. If I put a four per cent variance in a slide with no explanation, somebody senior reads shrinkage and the next question is about security cameras, and then we spend money on the wrong thing entirely. So I would rather present the three pieces first and the total last. I have put the working in the where house folder with the queries beside it so anybody can re run the numbers themselves rather than taking my word for it.

Working through the restructure of the reference section before I write any of it, and this is thinking aloud rather than a plan anybody should act on yet. The problem with the current reference is not that it is wrong, it is that it is organised the way the code is organised rather than the way a reader arrives. Everything lives under the module that implements it, which is perfect if you already know which module you need and useless otherwise, and the search log says most people arrive with a task rather than a module name. The top three searches last month were about authentication tokens, about rate limits, and about retrying a failed request, and none of those three is a module. So the shape I want is a task oriented reference on top of the generated one, not instead of it. The generated pages stay exactly as they are, because they are complete and they are accurate and they cost nothing to maintain, and I have watched two previous attempts at a handwritten reference rot within a release. What I add is a layer of task pages that link into the generated pages, and the rule for a task page is that it answers one question, contains at least one complete runnable example, and never explains a concept that has its own page. The token page is the one I want to write first because it is the one people get wrong, and they get it wrong in a specific way. They read that a token expires in an hour, they write a refresh loop on a timer, and then the loop and the clock drift apart under load and they see authentication failures that look random. The correct pattern is to refresh on a failure rather than on a schedule, and that pattern is currently documented in a sentence in the middle of the errors page. Rate limits are the second one and the issue there is that we document the limit but not the header that tells you how much of it you have left, so everybody implements a fixed delay and the fixed delay is either too slow or too aggressive. Retries are the third and that page does not exist at all, which is an embarrassment given the number of support tickets that end with somebody being told to add a backoff. On the examples themselves, every one has to run against the sandbox with no edits beyond a key, and I want them tested in the pipeline rather than reviewed by eye, because an example that no longer compiles is worse than no example, it costs the reader twenty minutes and it costs us their trust. That means the examples live in the repository as real files and get pulled into the page at build time rather than being pasted into the text, which is a build change and needs somebody who is not me to agree to it. Last thing, migration. Nothing gets deleted and no address changes in the first pass. The task pages are additive, they go in the navigation above the generated section, and if the search log in three months says people are still landing on the generated pages first then the experiment failed and we have lost nothing but my time.

The customer reported that their point of sale terminals were dropping the connection to our service for a few seconds at a time, several times an hour, always in the afternoon and never in the morning. First contact was Tuesday and the first thing I did was the thing we always do, which is ask them to reproduce it with the diagnostic build so we get timestamps we can trust, and to their credit they did that within a day. What came back was interesting. The drops are real, they are between four and nine seconds, and they line up almost exactly with a scheduled job on their side that pushes the price file. The price file is about eleven megabytes and it goes out over the same link the terminals use, and the link is not as fat as the customer believes it is, because I asked them for the circuit details and what they have is not what they are paying for. So my working theory by Wednesday was that this is congestion on their side and not a fault in our service at all. Then it got complicated. New paragraph. They pushed the price file at a quiet hour as a test, deliberately, and the terminals dropped anyway, which killed my theory in one message. So I went back to the timestamps and looked at what else is common to the afternoon, and the answer is the number of terminals actually transacting, which roughly triples after two o'clock. When I plotted drops against concurrent sessions rather than against time of day, the relationship is much cleaner, and there is a step at about forty concurrent sessions where the drops start. Forty is not a number that should mean anything, but it is very close to a connection pool limit in the version of the client library they are running, which is two majors behind. I have not proved that yet. What would prove it is either a packet capture at the moment of a drop, which they are nervous about because of card data, or a test with the current library on a single site, which they can do and which I have asked for. My recommendation for the next shift is to keep pushing gently for the single site upgrade test and to resist the urge to blame their circuit in writing, because the quiet hour test already showed the circuit is not the whole story and if we put it in a formal note we will have to walk it back. Also please do not close the parent case even if the child cases go quiet, because this customer measures us on the parent case and closing it early reads as us declaring victory. The account manager has a call with them Friday morning and wants a one line status, and the honest one line is that we have a strong lead, a limited scope test requested, and no fix yet.

Right, writing this down while I still remember the shape of it, because the postmortem is on Monday and I do not trust myself to reconstruct the order later. The symptom was that requests to the pricing service started timing out at about twenty past nine, but only the ones that came through the mobile gateway, which is why the dashboards looked fine for the first quarter of an hour. The pool on the pricing side has thirty connections and the mobile gateway holds a request open while it waits on a second call downstream, so thirty slow mobile requests are enough to starve every other caller on the box. That is not a new fact about the system, it is written in the runbook, and we still walked into it. What was new is why the downstream call got slow, and that turns out to be a migration somebody ran on the currency table at nine fifteen, which took a lock for about four minutes. Four minutes of a held lock on a table that every pricing lookup reads is enough to fill the pool, and once the pool is full the retries make it worse, because our client retries three times with no backoff at all. I have checked and the retry policy has been like that since the service was written, so this was always going to happen the first time anything downstream got slow. The fix I want to argue for is a separate pool for the mobile path and and a real backoff on the client.

Right, this is the focaccia written down because I am tired of explaining it to whoever is on mornings, and every time I explain it I say it slightly differently and then I get annoyed when it comes out slightly differently. The dough is not the hard part. The hard part is that the dough wants more time than the rota gives it, and everybody tries to fix that with more yeast, and more yeast is why the last three trays tasted of beer. So the first thing to understand is that we make it the night before, always, and if somebody has not made it the night before then we do not have focaccia that day and we put something else on the board. That is not me being difficult, it is that a four hour focaccia is a different bread and the people who come back for it will notice. The flour is the strong one in the paper sack and not the tipo zero zero, and the water is more than you think, about eighty five percent, so the dough will look wrong in the mixer and you have to trust it. Oil in the tray, oil on your hands, oil on top before it goes in, and do not be careful with it. The salt on top is the course one and not the fine one, because fine salt dissolves and you taste nothing, and it goes on after the second prove and never before, since salt on the surface pulls the water out and the top goes leathery. Now the order for the morning person. First take the tray out of the fridge and leave it somewhere warm for two hours. Second dimple it with your fingers all the way down to the bottom of the tray. Third put the rosemary and the salt on and give it another twenty minutes. Fourth put it in at two forty for eighteen minutes and turn the tray once. That is the whole thing, and the only part that changes is the oven, because the one at the back runs hot and wants two thirty. The other thing that goes wrong is the tomato version. If you are doing the tomato one the tomatoes goes on before the second prove and not after, otherwise they sit on top and burn before the bread underneath is done, and half the tray comes out with black skins on it. The cherry tomatoes from the market are better than the tinned for this and they cost less in season, so use them while we can. And whoever is on mornings should check the yeast on a Monday, because we had a week where nothing rose properly and it turned out the yeast had been open since before I went away, and nobody thought to look at it because the tub was still half full. The last thing is that it goes on the board as focaccia and not as flat bread. I have seen it written up as flat bread twice and it is not the same thing, and the person who wrote it that way knows who they are. If we run out by two then write it off the board rather than making a second batch in a hurry, because the hurried one is the one people remember.

Okay, incident write up for the certificate expiry on Tuesday, and I want the timeline right because two of the numbers in the chat channel are wrong and they are wrong in a way that makes us look better than we were. The first user report came in at zero seven fifty, sorry, zero seven fifteen, and I am being pedantic about that because our own monitoring did not fire until zero eight zero two, so the gap between a customer knowing and us knowing was forty seven minutes and not twelve. That gap is the actual finding. Everything else in this write up is detail. What expired was the intermediate on the internal mesh, not the public certificate, which is why the status page stayed green and why the first three people to look at it concluded there was nothing wrong. Internal traffic between the two payment services failed closed, which is correct behaviour, and the retry logic in front of it kept the error rate under the alert threshold for the first half hour by spreading the failures out. So the alert threshold hid it, the retries hid it, and the status page hid it, and all three of those are things we chose. On the certificate itself, the renewal job had been failing for nine days. It failed silently because it writes its result to a log stream nobody reads and it exits zero regardless. The reason it was failing is that the hostname in the mesh config gained a trailing dot in a change three weeks ago, which is legal and which the mesh accepts, but the certificate authority client compares the requested name against its own record as a plain string and the dot made it a mismatch. So the request was rejected every night, and every night the job said nothing. I want to be careful here because there are two separate mistakes and only one of them is interesting. The uninteresting one is that somebody added a dot. That is fine, it is a correct configuration, and I would not ask anybody to stop doing it. The interesting one is that a job whose entire purpose is to prevent an outage can fail for nine days without anybody knowing. Recovery took thirty one minutes from the point somebody looked at the right log, and twenty of those thirty one were spent finding who had permission to run the renewal by hand. That is the second finding. On follow ups, I have opened three tickets and I am going to describe them rather than list them because they are not equally important. The one that matters is alerting on the age of the certificate rather than on the job exiting non zero, because the job exits zero when it fails. The second is the permission thing, which is a five minute change and a two week conversation. The third is that the internal mesh should have its own status signal, and I am least confident about that one because it is the kind of thing that gets built and then ignored. The roll back plan we did not need but should write down anyway is that the mesh can run in permissive mode for about an hour before the compliance people notice, and that is worth knowing at three in the morning.

Right, this is the draft of the troubleshooting page for the log agent and I am dictating it so I can hear whether the ordering makes sense before I write it properly. Start with the symptom the reader actually has, not with the architecture, because nobody arrives at a troubleshooting page wanting to learn how the agent works. The symptom is almost always the same, which is that events appear in the console with the wrong timestamp or they appear split across several entries. The split case is the one people misdiagnose. What has happened is that the application wrote a multi line message and the agent read each physical line as a separate event, because by default the agent has no idea that a stack trace is one thing. So the fix is the multiline pattern in the agent config, and the pattern has to match the first line of the event rather than the continuation, which is the opposite of what most people try first, new paragraph. I want to say that twice in the page because it is the single most common mistake. If your application writes a line break inside a JSON field the same thing happens for a different reason, and the fix there is not a multiline pattern at all, it is telling the agent the input is JSON so it stops treating physical lines as boundaries. Those two look identical in the console and they need different fixes, so the page needs a way for the reader to tell them apart quickly. The quickest test I know is whether the first fragment is valid JSON on its own. If it is, you have the multiline problem. If it is not, you have the JSON problem. On the timestamp case, there are three causes and I want them in this order because that is the order of likelihood and not the order of interest. The first is that the agent is parsing the timestamp with the wrong format string and falling back to ingestion time, which looks like every event arriving at once. The second is a genuine clock problem on the host, which is rare now but still happens on the older virtual machines. The third is that somebody has two agents running on the same file, which produces duplicates with slightly different times and is by far the most confusing to look at. I have seen the third one three times and every time it took a day. On the structure of the page, I do not want a decision tree diagram. So these are my notes for the referee report on the manuscript about the survey instrument, and I am dictating them because I think more clearly out loud and because the report is due Thursday. My overall position is that the paper should be revised rather than rejected, and that the revision is larger than the authors will want to hear. The central claim is that the shortened instrument measures the same construct as the full instrument, and the evidence offered for that is a correlation of point eight seven between the two total scores in a single sample. That is not nothing and it is also not what the claim requires. Two instruments can correlate at that level while disagreeing about a substantial minority of individual respondents, which is exactly what matters if the instrument is going to be used to decide anything about a person rather than about a population. The authors know this. There is a sentence in the discussion that almost says it. What is missing is any analysis at the level of the individual case, and the data to do it are clearly in hand. The second problem is the reporting of the item statistics. Table three gives means and standard deviations for all thirty items, and for six of the items the value in the standard deviation column is truncated in the printed version, so the entry literally ends in dot dot dot. I assume that is a typesetting accident rather than a decision, but I cannot check the six items I most want to check, and those six are the ones the authors dropped. I have flagged it as a required correction rather than a criticism. The third problem is a real one and I am not sure the authors can fix it within a revision. The sample is a convenience sample from two institutions and the paper describes it as representative of the sector. It is not, and the two institutions differ from the sector on the one variable that the instrument is most sensitive to. I would ask them to either drop the representativeness claim entirely or add a second sample, and I expect they will drop the claim, which is the honest outcome. There is also a smaller thing in the data appendix that I want to mention because it will bite whoever tries to replicate this. The supplementary file is comma separated and three of the free text response fields contain a comma without quoting, so the file does not parse in any standard reader and the column count varies by row. I only found the real values by opening it in a text editor. That should be fixed before publication regardless of what happens to the rest of the paper. Should I say all of that in the report or raise the appendix issue with the editor separately, because it is the kind of thing that gets lost in a long report and it is also the one thing that is unambiguously wrong. On the writing I have very little to say. The paper is clear, the notation is consistent, and the literature review is fair to the work it disagrees with, which is rarer than it should be.

Writing up the flaky test properly because I have now been asked about it three times. The test is not flaky in the way people mean when they say flaky. It fails about one run in nine and it fails for a reason, which is that it asserts on the order of two rows that come back from a query with no order by clause. On the developer machines the planner picks a sequential scan and the rows come back in insertion order every time, so it passes locally forever. On the build machine the table is larger because the seed job runs twice, the planner picks the index, and the order changes. That is the whole mechanism and there is nothing intermittent about it. I have not fixed it yet and I want to say why. The obvious fix is to add an order by to the query inside the test, which makes the test pass and hides the fact that the production code also depends on that order in one place, in the export path, where it has never been noticed because the export is small. So the fix is in the production query, not in the test, and then the test can keep asserting on order because the order will be real. I have opened a separate ticket for the seed job running twice, since that is a build configuration problem rather than a test problem and it is also why the build machine has been slowing down since June. None of this is urgent this week, but I would rather nobody quarantined the test in the meantime, because a quarantined test is how this stops being anybody's problem.

Handover on the bundle size work because I am off next week and somebody will ask about it on Tuesday. The number everybody quotes is the six hundred and forty kilobyte figure from the dashboard, and that number is the gzipped main chunk only, so it is both correct and misleading. I have put the honest number in the readme under performance so nobody has to rediscover it. The work I actually finished is the locale split. Before, we shipped every locale in one file because the loader in src/i18n/index.ts imported the whole directory, so a user in Seoul downloaded French. Now the loader takes the locale from the html lang attribute and does a dynamic import of src/i18n/locales/ko.json, and the fallback path when the locale is missing loads en.json rather than throwing. That one change is about a hundred and eighty kilobytes for most users and it is already merged. The work I started and did not finish is the vendor chunk, and this is the bit I would rather explain here than leave in a ticket. The chunk is large because of two libraries, and only one of them is really needed at first paint. So the sequence is, do the four other places first, then remove the dependency, then the hand written helper is the only date code we have. If you do it in the other order you will get a review comment about consistency and you will deserve it. The second library is the chart one, and that one is straightforward, it is only used on the reporting route and the route is already lazy. The reason it is in the vendor chunk anyway is a stale entry in the manual chunks list in vite.config.ts, which names it explicitly and therefore hoists it. Delete that line and the bundle analyser will show it moving to the route chunk, and that is worth about ninety kilobytes for anyone who never opens reporting, which is most people. I have not deleted it myself because I could not get the analyser to run against the production config on my machine and I do not want to push a bundle change I have not measured. Everything I have described is in the branch called perf/locale-split, the merged part is on main already, and the two unfinished pieces are the last two commits which are marked as work in progress in the commit messages.

Right, this is for the group that arrives on Sunday and honestly it is more of a warning than a briefing, so send it as it is, do not make it sound like a brochure. The trek is not hard. I want to be clear about that first because people arrive terrified after reading the internet. It is eleven days of walking uphill slowly, and slowly is the whole trick, and the people who struggle are almost never the unfit ones, they are the fit ones who go too fast on day two because they feel great. If you feel great on day two you are going too fast. The bit nobody warns you about is not the altitude, it is the food and the boredom. You will eat the same three things for eleven days and by day six you will have strong opinions about garlic soup. Bring something that tastes of home, a stupid amount of it, and be generous with it, because the person who shares snacks on day seven becomes everybody's favourite human. Bring a book you actually want to read, not a book you think you should read on a mountain, because there is nothing to do after six in the evening and the electricity is a rumour. The other real thing is the money. Bring cash, more than you think, in small notes, because the machines at the bottom do not work half the time and the machines further up do not exist. Everything gets more expensive the higher you go for the extremely good reason that somebody carried it there on their back. Do not haggle about that. Haggle about nothing, actually, at least not with anybody carrying a load. The kit list is the same as it has always been and I am not repeating it, but two things get ignored every single group. One is that your boots need to have been worn before you get on the plane, and worn means walked in, not tried on. Every trip somebody arrives with boots so new they squeak and by day three they cannot put their heels down. The other is the sleeping bag rating. You will be warm in the day and genuinely cold at four in the morning at the top two lodges, and no amount of enthusiasm fixes a thin bag. Rent a better one in town, it costs about the same as two coffees at home. On the altitude, we go slowly, we take the acclimatisation day even if everybody feels brilliant, and nobody gets to be brave about a headache. Tell me about a headache. Tell me about it early, tell me about it even if you think it is nothing, and I will almost always tell you it is nothing, and the one time it is not nothing is the reason I ask. That is the only rule I will be strict about the entire eleven days. Everything else, wear what you like, walk how you like, take four hundred photographs of the same mountain like everybody does, and do not apologise for being slow because slow is correct.

The change is in the retry layer and is bigger than I wanted it to be. The original bug was tiny and the fix kept pulling on things. The reported problem was that uploads over about 40 MB failed roughly one time in nine on mobile networks and the failure looked like a success in our logs, which is why it took three weeks for anyone to notice. What actually happens is that the client streams the file in 4 MB chunks, and if a chunk times out the client retries it, and the retry uses a fresh signed URL, but the server was keying the assembly by URL rather than by upload id, so the retried chunk landed in a second half finished assembly and the first one was never cleaned up. Then the finaliser saw a complete set of chunks for the wrong assembly, returned 200, and we stored a file that was missing about 8 MB out of the middle. The reason it looked fine is that our checksum was computed client side before the upload and stored alongside it, and nobody was comparing it to anything on the way back out. So there are really three changes in here. The keying is now on upload id and the signed URL is just a credential, which is a nine line change and is the actual bug fix. Then the finaliser verifies the assembled length against the declared length before it returns, and refuses with a 409 if they differ, which is another twenty lines and is the thing that would have caught this in week one. And then the third change is the one I want you to argue with me about, which is that I added a stored checksum comparison on read, behind a flag, defaulting off, because I do not know what it costs on the big files and I did not want to find out in production on a Friday. I have it running on the staging bucket with the flag on and the read path is about 4 per cent slower on a 200 MB object and unmeasurably different under 10 MB, but staging has one client and production has forty thousand so I do not trust that number very far. Use bullet points for the testing section. I wrote a test that uploads six chunks, kills the third one twice, and asserts the assembled length. I wrote a second test that asserts the finaliser returns 409 when a chunk is missing entirely rather than 200. I wrote a third test that runs the whole flow with the read checksum flag on and off and asserts identical bytes out. All three fail on the old code and pass on the new code, which I checked by stashing the fix rather than by trusting myself. What I did not test is the concurrent case where two clients upload the same upload id, because I could not make that happen without writing a fake client and I ran out of appetite, and I think it is genuinely unlikely given the id comes from a server side create call, but it is not impossible and somebody should say so in review. There is also a migration question I have not solved. Any file already stored with a short assembly is still short, and this change does not find them or fix them. I can write a job that walks the bucket and compares stored length to declared length, and on the numbers I have that is about 2.1 million objects and maybe six hours, but I would rather do that as a separate change with its own review than bolt it onto this one. The logging is different too, and I should flag that because it will show up in dashboards. The old code logged an assembly complete line per URL, so a retried upload logged twice and our success count was inflated by however many retries happened, which is why the graph looked healthy. Now it logs once per upload id, so the absolute number of successes will appear to drop by something like 3 per cent overnight without anything getting worse. Somebody will ask about that on Monday and the answer is that the old number was wrong. Deployment is safe in either order because the new keying is backwards compatible with in flight uploads, or I believe it is, and the reason I believe it is that the URL is still accepted and ignored rather than rejected. I would deploy the server first, watch the 409 rate for an hour, and then turn the read flag on for internal accounts only. If the 409 rate is anything other than near zero then we have a second bug and I want to know before the flag goes anywhere near a customer.

Okay, this is everything I know about the tender for the community hall roof, and I am putting it in one message because three people have now asked me the same questions in a slightly different order. The notice went up on the fourteenth and the closing date is the twenty eighth at four in the afternoon, which is a Friday, and the office shuts at five so there is no argument to be had about arriving at ten past. The work is the full roof on the old hall, which is the one behind the water tank and not the newer building that everyone assumes, and if you are looking at the drawing then it is the structure marked with a dot on the north west corner, because that dot is how they distinguish the two on every sheet in the file. The scope as written is stripping the existing sheets, replacing the purlins where they are rotten, which is most of them on the north side, laying new sheets, and making good the parapet where the old fixings have pulled through. There is a line in the scope about guttering that is ambiguous, because it says make good existing guttering and the existing guttering is not really there any more, so I would price for replacement and say clearly in the covering note that you have done so, rather than pricing for nothing and arguing about it later. The bid documents cost 2,000 rupees and you collect them from the ward office in person between ten and one, and they will not send them, and they will not accept a photograph of a receipt, and yes somebody has tried. Bring the firm's registration and the VAT certificate and a copy of the last tax clearance, and bring two copies of each because the clerk keeps one. The bid security is 5 per cent of your quoted amount and it has to be a bank guarantee valid for ninety days from the closing date, not a cheque, and the ninety days catches people out because most of the standard forms come out at sixty. If you need to ask them anything formally then write to tenders dot office at kavre municipality dot gov dot np and copy the ward secretary, and expect three working days for a reply, and do not rely on the phone number in the notice because it rings in a room nobody sits in. Anything they tell you verbally is worth nothing at the evaluation, so if a clarification matters, get it in writing or price around it. On the evaluation itself, it is lowest evaluated bid rather than lowest bid, which in practice with this office has meant that they do look at the technical submission and they do disqualify on missing documents, and last year two of the five bidders were thrown out on paperwork before any prices were opened. So the boring part is the part that decides it. The technical submission wants three similar works in the last five years with completion certificates, and similar has been read generously here before, so a school roof counts, and a shed does not. It wants the site engineer's licence and a signed statement that the engineer will be present, and they have asked for that engineer by name on site during a visit, so do not put down somebody who is in another district all week. On the price, the quantities in the bill are measured from the drawing and the drawing is from 2009, and the roof has been patched twice since, so the sheet count is low by my estimate by about 8 per cent and the purlin count is low by more than that. You are bidding on their quantities, so the honest way to handle it is to price their quantities and flag the variance in the covering note, because raising it after award is a fight you lose slowly. There is a site visit on the twentieth at eleven, and it is not mandatory but the people who skip it are the people who get the purlin count wrong, and the caretaker will open the ceiling hatch if you ask him nicely and bring your own torch. Take photographs of the north side from inside, because that is the evidence you will want if there is a variation claim later. Payment terms are 30 per cent on mobilisation against a guarantee, 50 per cent on progress certified by their engineer, and the rest on final measurement, and the final 20 per cent has historically taken four to five months to arrive, so please price your cash flow honestly rather than pretending that money comes in October. The retention is 5 per cent held for a year. My overall read is that it is a reasonable job at a fair size for a small firm, the office is slow but not difficult, and the two ways people lose it here are missing documents and the guttering line, and both of those are free to get right.
